title: Substitution
hook: the Reformers stressed Christ bearing the penalty in our place (Isaiah 53:5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, satisfaction: Anselm's ledger, a debt we owe and can't pay. Your line was he paid what we owed. What did you pay forward? Day one thousand eighty-four.

A prison door swings open in Jerusalem, and a man named Barabbas walks out into the daylight. The Gospels tell this moment. Mark calls him a man held with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising. He was in chains. Then the Roman governor lets him go. Mark says Pilate "released Barabbas unto them, and delivered Jesus, when he had scourged him, to be crucified." One man walks free. Another goes to the cross. The Gospels never tell us what Barabbas did next, or whether he ever stood near Golgotha and looked up. But some readers have stood in his sandals ever since. Today's word: substitution.

Substitution means one in the place of another. Christians reading the cross this way go back to a song in Isaiah, about a servant who suffers: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." Notice the little words. For our. Upon him. The wounds belong to one, the healing to others. The first letter of Peter picks up the same song: Christ "his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree." Here's what's new compared with yesterday. Anselm said a wrong is either made good or punished, and put the cross on the payment side. The Reformers, Luther and Calvin among them, read the same texts and stressed the other side. The penalty for sin was real, and Christ bore it, in our place. Paul says it in one sharp line to the Corinthians: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." Luther called this a happy exchange: Christ takes what is ours, and gives us what is his. Some who hold this picture speak of it as their peace: the verdict has already been carried. Other Christians hold it more lightly, or worry it can sound like a Father punishing an unwilling Son. Those who hold it close answer that Father and Son act as one, out of the same love: God himself carries the cost. Churches weigh this picture differently. At its heart is Barabbas, and the open door.

Here's the practice: stand where Barabbas stood. Settle, and breathe. Picture the door open in front of you, the daylight outside. Now think of something you carry that you can't put down by yourself: a wrong you did, a weight you can't fix. Name it plainly. If you pray, you can thank God for bearing what you couldn't. If you don't, just notice what it would be like to walk through that door with your hands empty. Breathe out. The bell holds the time.
Substitution. One in the place of another: Christ bearing the penalty of sin so that others go free.
Your line: in my place. Today, take one small burden for someone else without being asked: a chore, a blame, a long wait. Day one thousand eighty-four.

howItsDone: In Reformed, Lutheran and evangelical churches, sermons, hymns and communion prayers speak of Christ dying in the believer's place, and some churches read Isaiah 53 during Holy Week.

notes: Barabbas appears in Matthew 27, Mark 15, Luke 23 and John 18; the script says only 'the Gospels tell this moment' under the claims rule.

Mark 15:7 paraphrased: Barabbas 'lay bound with them that had made insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the insurrection'. The script says 'held with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising'. Confirm.
The hook avoids naming the crowd's role to keep Rome's responsibility clear; Pilate releases and delivers. Confirm this is fair to the Gospel accounts.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced claims that Barabbas was waiting for a Roman cross and that Jesus carried the cross meant for him (hook, screen head, fork setup, and the next day's review now say only that another went to the cross); lowercased the word in the hook.
'Luther and Calvin among them' and the summary of the Reformers stressing penalty: standard but historical; confirm under the claims rule.
Luther's 'happy exchange' (froehlicher Wechsel) is from The Freedom of a Christian; paraphrased. Confirm.
Objections (a Father punishing an unwilling Son) and the reply (Father and Son act as one) given without ranking; confirm fairness.
